segments.text: Memory for Predicting Trust in Conversational Agents
segments.label: human

segments.text: Abstract-Predicting user trust in conversational agents remains a significant challenge. Most existing models fail to capture both the temporal dynamics of trust formation and the nuanced interplay between emotional, behavioral, and contextual signals. To address this, we present ConTrust, a deep learning architecture specifically designed for the Conversational Trust Dataset, which contains 3,909 conversations (26,329 turns total, with 12,569 agent turns annotated for trust). Unlike traditional regression or shallow learning approaches, ConTrust integrates six key innovations. First, a trust-aware self-attention mechanism adaptively weights conversational cues based on their trust relevance. Second, an LSTM-based conversation memory module models longitudinal trust evolution. Third, we fuse textual, temporal, and behavioral features through multi-modal integration. Fourth, hierarchical attention captures dependencies at both turn and conversation levels. Fifth, multi-task learning jointly optimizes trust, emotion, and engagement predictions. Sixth, adaptive loss weighting dynamically balances these competing objectives. Extensive evaluations demonstrate ConTrust's substantial improvements over established baselines. While ensemble methods achieved R²=0.946 (RMSE=0.401), and strong learners like Random Forest (R²=0.944) and XGBoost (R²=0.938) performed competitively, ConTrust reaches R²=0.982 with RMSE=0.248. Crucially, 90% of predictions fall within ±0.5 error—a clear advance in trust modeling. Beyond these metrics, ConTrust offers interpretability by revealing how trust evolves with sentiment polarity, emotional congruence, and engagement intensity. This research contributes a scalable, domain-adaptable framework for trust prediction, establishing ConTrust as a foundation for reliable conversational agents in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, education, and customer support. Keywords-ConTrust, conversational trust prediction, trust-aware attention, conversation memory, multi-modal fusion, hierarchical attention, multi-task learning, adaptive loss weighting, deep learning, human-AI trust

segments.text: I Introduction
segments.label: human

segments.text: The degree to which users trust conversational systems fundamentally shapes their willingness to rely on automated agents for decision-making, assistance, and emotionally sensitive exchanges. While early research prioritized syntactic correctness and task completion [1][2], more recent work reveals a different picture: user acceptance hinges on perceived reliability, emotional responsiveness, and consistency maintained across time [3][4]. Interestingly, dissatisfaction often traces back to seemingly minor conversational missteps-delayed responses, emotionally misaligned phrasing, or overly generic engagement behavior [5][6]. Traditional supervised models, trained on isolated utterances, have consistently struggled with trust signals precisely because trust accumulates gradually rather than emerging from single turns [7][8]. As conversational agents proliferate across healthcare, educational support, advisory systems, and assistive technologies, we urgently need granular models that understand both message content and the trajectories of entire interactions [9][10].
segments.label: ai_generated

segments.text: A key limitation lies in existing datasets: they rarely offer explicit annotations for trust evolution, emotional valence, or engagement dynamics. Benchmarks designed for intent recognition or casual chit-chat evaluation almost never incorporate temporal indicators, behavioral markers, or longitudinal discourse context [11][12]. Generic turn-level annotations provide coarse labels, yet they fail to capture how psychological impressions shift with response timeliness, tone, or dialogue pacing [13][14]. When researchers retrofit trust estimators onto legacy corpora, the results often gloss over the nuanced interdependence between emotion, sentiment, and credibility cues. Even worse, studies limited to textual features completely miss delayed responses, perceived responsiveness, and fluctuating conversational involvement-all critical factors for trust assessment under realistic interaction conditions [15][16]. To model trust as a cumulative, contextually grounded construct rather than a post-hoc outcome, we need structurally rich datasets with layered annotations. Recent work in multi-modal learning offers a promising direction, demonstrating that merging linguistic sequences with behavioral traces, engagement markers, and temporal features substantially improves performance [17][18]. Architectures employing cross-attention, hierarchical encoders, and memory components have already shown success in sentiment interpretation, dialogue outcome prediction, and empathy recognition. However, trust represents a distinct relational dimension-one shaped by perceived competence, communication style, and emotional coherence across successive turns. Multi-goal interactions involving varied agent profiles demand systems that track both immediate cues and broader conversational arcs. By enriching trust annotations with emotional signals, sentiment shifts, latency data, and interaction depth, predictive frameworks can finally reflect the subtleties of real conversational judgment. Such a system could approximate, for instance, how users weigh early misalignments against later recovery efforts, or how stable tone coupled with low latency cultivates confidence across turns. Building architectures that model trust holistically requires supervisory signals capturing both immediate response quality and accrued conversational credibility [19][20]. Hybrid models combining memory mechanisms with attention-based feature integration exploit trust-related annotations far more effectively than single-task regressors constrained to surface patterns. Emotion recognition and engagement estimation function best as auxiliary signals that refine latent representations rather than distract from the primary trust prediction task. Integrating losses across multiple tasks encourages the model to learn shared regularities-particularly valuable in dialogues where emotional alignment and responsiveness directly influence trust trajectories. That said, without adaptive balancing of task contributions during training, performance can easily skew toward dominant signals while neglecting subtle yet trust-critical cues.

Through adaptive loss weighting and cross-modal fusion, ConTrust learns to balance competing objectives, addressing key limitations of prior single-dimensional trust models. This design enables generalization across diverse dialogue contexts, offering a scalable framework for real-time trust estimation within conversational AI ecosystems.

segments.text: 3.1 Dataset Preparation​
segments.label: human

segments.text: We previously introduced the Conversational Trust Dataset specifically to model trust in conversational agents. This addresses a critical gap: the lack of large-scale, ecologically valid corpora capturing both linguistic and behavioral signals that underpin human–AI trust dynamics. Conventional dialogue datasets focus primarily on intent recognition or task completion; ours was explicitly designed to reflect multi-dimensional trust cues across real-world conversational contexts. The dataset contains 3,909 multi-turn dialogues with 26,329 conversational turns, including 12,569 annotated agent responses. A panel of 15 trained annotators evaluated each response using a standardized 7-point Likert scale across four trust dimensions: competence, benevolence, integrity, and overall trustworthiness. Inter-annotator agreement exceeded κ=0.75, confirming annotation robustness. Beyond trust labels, we incorporated seven discrete emotions, sentiment polarity scores, response latency measures, and engagement metrics such as dialogue length, turn-taking balance, and emotional entropy. These features ensure the dataset captures not only surface-level linguistic performance but also the temporal, affective, and relational factors that shape trust [26]. Conversations were drawn from 35 scenarios spanning healthcare, technical support, travel planning, and open-domain queries. Agent responses originated from 23 distinct conversational models with diverse training paradigms, representing behaviors from highly-aligned instruction-tuned models to less predictable base models. For this research, we partitioned the dataset into 3,127 training and 782 validation conversations, maintaining balance across trust levels and emotional contexts. segments.text: VI Conclusion
segments.label: human

segments.text: Trust remains a cornerstone of sustainable human–AI interaction, particularly as conversational agents transition from informational tools to emotionally and socially responsive partners. This study introduced ConTrust, a novel deep learning framework that models trust as an evolving, context-dependent phenomenon rather than a static attribute. By integrating Trust-Aware Self-Attention, Conversation Memory, and Multi-Modal Fusion mechanisms, ConTrust holistically captures linguistic, temporal, and behavioral signals within multi-turn dialogues. Experimental evaluations conducted on the Conversational Trust Dataset—comprising over 3,900 annotated conversations and 26,000 dialogue turns—demonstrated the framework’s superior predictive fidelity, achieving R² = 0.982 and RMSE = 0.248, with 90% of trust predictions falling within a ±0.5 margin of error. Beyond numerical performance, the framework provides interpretability and psychological validity by revealing how emotional alignment, response latency, and engagement intensity influence human trust trajectories. The Bi-LSTM-based Conversation Memory Module proved especially effective in capturing longitudinal trust evolution, validating that temporal continuity and sequential coherence are essential determinants of trust perception. Similarly, the Adaptive Loss Weighting (ALW) mechanism ensured balanced learning across trust, emotion, and engagement tasks, enabling ConTrust to generalize across diverse dialogue contexts such as healthcare, education, and customer service. From an operational standpoint, the introduction of ConTrust-Fast, a lightweight variant with a 60% parameter reduction, demonstrated that computational efficiency need not compromise trust-prediction accuracy—achieving comparable R² values (0.972–0.98) with significantly lower latency. This underscores the scalability of the proposed architecture for real-time trust assessment in production environments and embedded conversational systems. Looking forward, future research will explore cross-domain transfer learning, multilingual adaptation, and reinforcement-driven trust calibration, wherein agents dynamically adjust their conversational strategies based on real-time trust feedback. Integrating explainable AI (XAI) modules into ConTrust will further enhance transparency, allowing users to understand why an agent is perceived as trustworthy or not. Ultimately, this work lays the foundation for designing ethically aligned, emotionally intelligent, and context-aware conversational agents that can build, sustain, and justify human trust in complex interaction ecosystems.
